Binomial nomenclature assigns each organism a standard, internationally recognised two-word scientific name, reducing confusion caused by different local names and languages.

Biodiversity is the variety of organisms in ecosystems. It supports ecosystem stability, food webs and essential ecological processes, while providing resources and services important to people and the planet.

Classification groups organisms by shared characteristics, making them easier to identify and study. It provides a common system for communication and helps show similarities and relationships among organisms.

The Linnaean system arranges organisms in nested groups, from broadest to most specific: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus and Species. Each successive rank contains organisms that are more similar and closely related. Domain is a broader rank used above kingdom in modern classification.
Archaea and Bacteria are unicellular prokaryotes without a nucleus. Bacterial cell walls contain peptidoglycan, but archaeal cell walls do not; some archaea are adapted to extreme environments.

Protista are mainly unicellular eukaryotes. Fungi are heterotrophs that absorb nutrients and have chitin cell walls. Plants are multicellular autotrophs with cellulose cell walls. Animals are multicellular heterotrophs without cell walls.

Viruses are acellular and lack the cellular structure of organisms in the three domains. They cannot carry out all life processes independently and reproduce only inside host cells, so they do not fit the classification of cellular life.
A scientific name has two words: the capitalised genus name followed by the lowercase species name. Both words are italicised in print or underlined separately when handwritten.
Incorrect classification can mislead researchers about an organism’s relationships and needs, causing errors in scientific studies, communication or conservation decisions.
